question: Combining Figure 2 (Page 3) and the Section 3 text on Page 4, how were the HumanEval problems split into difficulty buckets before training completed, which bucket is displayed in Figure 2, and on which difficulty bucket did GPT-4 underperform the registered scaling predictions?
expected_answer: According to Page 4 and Figure 2 (Page 3), before training completed, all but the 15 hardest HumanEval problems were split into 6 difficulty buckets based on the performance of smaller models. Figure 2 plots the 3rd easiest bucket (23 coding problems), while GPT-4 underperformed the registered predictions on the easiest bucket.

answer: The HumanEval problems were divided into six difficulty buckets (excluding the 15 hardest problems) based on how smaller models performed on them before training was finished. Figure 2 displays the results for the **3rd easiest bucket** (the third bucket from the easiest side) [gpt4-2023-techreport_p003_chart_01]. GPT‑4 underperformed the registered scaling predictions on the **easiest bucket** [gpt4-2023-techreport_p004_text_02].

[CHART: Figure 1 & Figure 2 | Page 3 | BBox (45, 55, 565, 680)]
- Figure 1 Title: OpenAI codebase next word prediction — Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models.
  Metric (y-axis): Final loss in Bits per word (range 1.0 to 6.0, lower is better) on an internal codebase dataset not in training set.
  X-axis: Training compute normalized so that GPT-4 = 1 (ticks: 100p, 10n, 1u, 100u, 0.01, 1). Series: Observed (dots) vs Prediction (dotted power-law fit to smaller models excluding GPT-4). GPT-4 final loss (~1.8 bits per word at compute=1) matches the power-law prediction.
- Figure 2 Title: Capability prediction on 23 coding problems — Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models on a subset of the HumanEval dataset (3rd easiest difficulty bucket).
  Metric (y-axis): -Mean Log Pass Rate (range 0 to 5). X-axis: Training compute normalized so that GPT-4 = 1 (ticks: 1u, 10u, 100u, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1). Power-law fit to smaller models accurately predicts GPT-4 pass rate.

[IMAGE_DIAGRAM: Table 17 | Page 37 | BBox (55, 55, 555, 720)]
- Visual Input Example (Table 17 — Pixel to Paper Summaries): Three page-screenshot images of the InstructGPT paper (including Figure 2 architecture diagram of the 3-step RLHF pipeline).
- User follow-up prompt on diagram: 'Could you explain the process described in Figure 2?'
- Three steps read from Figure 2 diagram in the screenshot:
  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): Collect labeler demonstration data of prompts and desired output behavior to fine-tune GPT-3.
  2. Reward model (RM) training: Collect human labeler rankings of several model outputs from best to worst to train the reward model.
  3. Reinforcement learning using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): Optimize the SFT policy against the reward model using PPO.

We registered predictions for GPT-4’s performance on HumanEval before training completed, using only information available prior to training. All but the 15 hardest HumanEval problems were split into 6 difficulty buckets based on the performance of smaller models. The results on the 3rd easiest bucket are shown in Figure 2, showing that the resulting predictions were very accurate for this subset of HumanEval problems where we can accurately estimate log(pass_rate) for several smaller models. Predictions on the other five buckets performed almost as well, the main exception being GPT-4 underperforming our predictions on the easiest bucket.

[CHART: Figure 3 | Page 4 | BBox (110, 340, 500, 620)]
- Figure 3 Title: Inverse scaling prize, hindsight neglect — Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models on the Hindsight Neglect task.
- X-axis (Model scale): ada -> babbage -> curie -> gpt-3.5 -> gpt-4.
- Y-axis: Accuracy (%, range 0 to 100, higher is better).
- Trend & Values: Performance decreases with scale from ada (~38%), babbage (~32%), curie (~22%) down to gpt-3.5 (~12%, inverse scaling), but GPT-4 reverses the inverse scaling trend and jumps to ~100% accuracy.

Figure 2. Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models. The metric is mean log pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval dataset. A power law fit to the smaller models (excluding GPT-4) is shown as the dotted line; this fit accurately predicts GPT-4’s performance. The x-axis is training compute normalized so that GPT-4 is 1.

We believe that accurately predicting future capabilities is important for safety. Going forward we plan to refine these methods and register performance predictions across various capabilities before large model training begins, and we hope this becomes a common goal in the field.
We tested GPT-4 on a diverse set of benchmarks, including simulating exams that were originally designed for humans.4 We did no specific training for these exams. A minority of the problems in the exams were seen by the model during training; for each exam we run a variant with these questions removed and report the lower score of the two. We believe the results to be representative. For further details on contamination (methodology and per-exam statistics), see Appendix C.

Having a sense of the capabilities of a model before training can improve decisions around alignment, safety, and deployment. In addition to predicting final loss, we developed methodology to predict more interpretable metrics of capability. One such metric is pass rate on the HumanEval dataset [43], which measures the ability to synthesize Python functions of varying complexity. We successfully predicted the pass rate on a subset of the HumanEval dataset by extrapolating from models trained with at most 1, 000× less compute (Figure 2).
For an individual problem in HumanEval, performance may occasionally worsen with scale. Despite these challenges, we find an approximate power law relationship −EP [log(pass_rate(C))] = α∗C−k

Certain capabilities remain hard to predict. For example, the Inverse Scaling Prize [44] proposed several tasks for which model performance decreases as a function of scale. Similarly to a recent result by Wei et al. [45], we find that GPT-4 reverses this trend, as shown on one of the tasks called Hindsight Neglect [46] in Figure 3.

Figure 3. Performance of GPT-4 and smaller models on the Hindsight Neglect task. Accuracy is shown on the y-axis, higher is better. ada, babbage, and curie refer to models available via the OpenAI API [47].
